terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where the same changes go to the old order screen and to a screen drawn from your store.

tasks.title: Keep the state in one place
tasks.description:
Implement `nextState(state, part)` and `createStore(initial)` with `getState()` and `setState(part)` in `src/store.js`.

- `nextState(state, part)` returns the state with the part joined in: each key of the part takes its new value, a key the state did not have is added, and every other key keeps the one it had
- only the top keys are joined: a part's `{ stock: { kind: 'kraft' } }` replaces the old `stock` whole
- `createStore(initial)` returns a new store whose state starts as `initial`; two stores never share their state
- `store.getState()` returns the state now
- `store.setState(part)` joins the part into the state; `nextState` does the joining, so `setState` can call it

The check makes its own stores with states of its own, changes them and reads them back, and calls `nextState` on its own.
nextSteps: Run `node src/try.js` and read the error under the old screen.
Write `nextState` first: a new object with the keys of the state, then the keys of the part.
In `createStore`, keep the state in a variable of that call and return an object with `getState` and `setState`.
Run the script again: the basket count should match the basket.
hints: A store is a variable and two functions that can reach it. A function written inside `createStore` keeps that variable for as long as the store exists.
Spreading two objects into a new one joins them: when both have a key, the one spread last wins. Which one should win here?
`return { ...state, ...part }` in `nextState`. In `createStore`: `let state = initial`, and return `{ getState: () => state, setState(part) { state = nextState(state, part) } }`.

tasks.title: Change it with a function
tasks.description:
Let `setState` take a function as well as a part, and refuse what is neither.

- `setState(fn)` calls `fn` once with the state now, and joins in the part it returns
- two changes in a row each start from what the one before left, so two `+1` functions add 2
- a part, or a part a function returns, that is not an object throws a `TypeError`, and the state stays as it was; `null` is not an object here
- `createStore` throws a `TypeError` when the first state is not an object

The check gives its stores functions of its own, notes what each function was called with, and tries `null`, numbers, text and a function that returns nothing.
nextSteps: Look at the lines in `src/try.js` that remove a line from the basket: they hand `setState` a function.
In `setState`, find out whether the change is a function. If it is, call it to get the part.
Before joining, make sure the part is an object, and throw a `TypeError` when it is not.
Do the same check on the first state in `createStore`.
hints: A change that depends on the state, like one more job, is safest as a function: the store hands it the state as it is at that moment.
`typeof change === 'function'` tells you which kind you have. For the part, `typeof part === 'object'` is true for `null` too, so check for `null` on its own.
`const part = typeof change === 'function' ? change(state) : change`, then `if (typeof part !== 'object' || part === null) throw new TypeError('...')` before `state = nextState(state, part)`.

tasks.title: Never change the old state
tasks.description:
Make every change build a new state object and leave the old one exactly as it was.

- after a change, `getState()` returns a new object, not the one it returned before
- a state someone read before the change keeps every value it had, and gains no new keys
- the object given to `createStore` is never changed
- `nextState(state, part)` returns a new object and changes neither `state` nor `part`

The check keeps the states it read before each change and compares them afterwards, and calls `nextState` with objects it watches.
nextSteps: Read "An old state never changes" in the lesson.
Look at how `nextState` builds its result: does it write into an object it was given?
Check that `setState` only ever replaces the state, and never writes into it.
hints: Code elsewhere may still hold a state it read a moment ago. If the store writes into that object, its values change under that code's feet.
`Object.assign(state, part)` and `state[key] = value` write into the old object. A new object made with `{ }` and spread leaves it alone.
`return { ...state, ...part }` builds a new object every time, and `state = nextState(state, part)` points the store at it without touching the old one.
